content: To effectively monitor progress in this area, it is essential to collect detailed data on the provision of health services in prisons and other closed settings. This data should be disaggregated by setting type (e.g., prisons versus community settings) to identify disparities in access to healthcare services and to evaluate whether the principle of equivalence of care is being upheld. Additionally, disaggregating data by geographic area is crucial for many countries to inform decisions about where services should be located. For instance, rural and urban areas may have distinct population characteristics and service provision challenges, necessitating tailored approaches. Setting targets for the indicators described earlier facilitates strategic, results-based planning to build an effective response to the HIV epidemic. Targets can be established for intervention and enabling environment indicators, such as availability, coverage, and quality of services, as well as for structural factors like legislative changes within a specific timeframe. These targets aim to reduce HIV risk sufficiently to control the epidemic and ensure appropriate management for those living with HIV. Outcome and impact indicators can also be targeted, focusing on reducing the incidence of HIV or sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and changing risk behaviors, such as increasing consistent condom use. These targets help identify specific areas requiring attention and the scale of programmatic responses needed. They also guide the design of actions to meet high-level commitments, such as those outlined in the United Nations General Assembly’s 2011 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS. While only one of the goals explicitly mentions a key population, the targets are broadly relevant to addressing HIV among key populations. For example, the 2011 Political Declaration set ambitious goals to be achieved by 2015, including reducing sexual transmission of HIV by 50%, halving HIV transmission among people who inject drugs, eliminating HIV infections among children, and reducing maternal deaths. Other goals included reaching 15 million people living with HIV with antiretroviral therapy, halving tuberculosis deaths among people living with HIV, closing the global AIDS resource gap, eliminating gender inequalities and gender-based violence, and eradicating HIV-related stigma, discrimination, and punitive laws. The complexity of factors influencing HIV risk and intervention impact means there is no universal formula for setting targets. Targets must reflect local factors, such as the nature of the HIV epidemic, the current stage of the response, available resources, and structural determinants of risk. Countries must undertake a collaborative process involving community-led organizations, government representatives, civil society, service providers, and clinicians to set realistic and achievable targets. This process should include assessing the current scale of the response, evaluating the availability, coverage, and quality of interventions, and determining enabling environmental factors. Available resources and capacity must also be assessed to establish a baseline for measuring future progress. Once the baseline is established, countries should estimate the potential scale-up of interventions within a set timeframe, considering available resources and technical capacity. Realistic, achievable target levels can then be defined, along with the time period for their achievement. Strengthening systems for program monitoring may be necessary to improve tracking of progress toward these targets. The effectiveness of interventions depends on several principles. Multiple interventions are more effective than single interventions alone, and high-quality interventions deliver greater impact. Greater levels of coverage are superior to lower levels, but the relationship between coverage and HIV risk reduction is not always linear. Higher HIV prevalence requires greater intervention coverage, and earlier introduction of interventions in an epidemic is more effective in controlling HIV spread. Countries should set intermediate targets to guide incremental progress toward achieving global goals, such as the UNAIDS Fast-Track Targets. These include ensuring that by 2020, 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed receive treatment, and 90% of those on treatment achieve viral suppression. By 2030, these targets should increase to 95%. Other Fast-Track Targets include reducing new HIV infections among adults in lowand middle-income countries to 500,000 per year by 2020 and 200,000 per year by 2030, and achieving zero discrimination by eliminating HIV-related discriminatory laws and policies. Global targets play a critical role in maintaining attention and action at the international level. Countries must decide how to translate these targets into national programs tailored to their local epidemic and context. Intermediate targets at the national level can guide incremental progress toward achieving these global goals. As new evidence emerges, indicative target levels may be revised to reflect updated knowledge and commitments. Indicators for assessing key factors related to the enabling environment, availability, coverage, and quality of health sector interventions, as well as the outcomes and impacts of efforts to address HIV among key populations, are essential. These indicators should be relevant to each key population, including men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Countries should develop programs and plans and measure progress for each key population separately. Auditing current legislation and policies is critical to identifying laws and practices that may negatively impact key populations or hinder efforts to address HIV. This process should involve government, civil society, and community-led networks. Where reforms are needed, processes for change should be identified and evaluated. Guidance on conducting legal environment assessments for HIV is available to support these efforts.
